On Monday France and Germany sent an astonishing letter to the European Commission with far-reaching proposals on how to deal with China’s increasingly intimidating export machine (without explicitly mentioning the country). 

It contains ideas on a “second-strike capability”—so that Brussels has the powers to hit back quickly at countries that retaliate when the EU imposes trade measures over allegedly unfair competition—and calls for economic diversification.

If implemented through the EU’s law-making apparatus, it would mark a dramatic shift in how the bloc intends to confront China. Tap the link in our bio to read why.

Photo: AFP via Getty Images

In recent years the Israeli government has invested vast sums in online psychological warfare, using AI tools to try to influence audiences in the Middle East and public opinion in the West. 

Some are now being used domestically.

“Fake videos aren’t the main concern,” says one expert. “They’re easy to spot. What’s much more threatening is the way AI is being used beneath the surface to slant information and to monitor and manipulate voters.”

Israeli tech outfits have developed swarms of bots masquerading as human voters. Tap the link in our bio to learn how these can push conversations online towards themes and views advantageous to whoever controls them.

Illustration: @tameemsankari

At the heart of British politics lies a paradox. Tax is forecast to reach the highest level since the 1940s. 

Yet most British workers do not pay much of it. The average single earner pays less tax on their earnings than most of their peers in the OECD, a club of rich countries.
 
They also pay less than they used to. How does the Treasury make the sums add up?

Tap the link in our bio to discover how new research shows that Britain overtaxes well-paid workers, to the benefit of average earners and the super-rich. 

Illustration: @simonbailly

October 6th marks exactly 50 years since the official end of the Cultural Revolution in China. There will be no big celebrations. 

The date is altogether too sensitive for the Communist Party, given its profound aversion to examining past errors. The party long ago rendered a negative verdict on the Cultural Revolution and has no interest in reopening old wounds.

But keeping silent about this momentous chapter in China’s history haunts not just its dwindling number of living victims, but the party itself. Tap the link in our bio to read why.

Illustration: @cornelia_illo

Worries about massive corporate scandals and hedge-fund blow-ups which would have once occupied investors’ attention for months, are steamrolled by the relentless, totalising and extraordinarily flexible machine that is American finance.

Its achievements in the past year alone are endless, from the largest-ever initial public offering (SpaceX) to the biggest bond issue in history (Amazon).

Each American’s patriotic duty is to keep spending and to keep betting: when a man is tired of American capital markets, he is surely tired of life itself.

All this brings to mind a speedball, that lethal combination of heroin and cocaine popular among rock stars a generation ago. Tap the link in our bio to find out whether this high will last.

Illustration: @brett.ryder.illustration

Most countries used to hoard foreign reserves defensively: they might need them to prop up the exchange rate in a crisis. 

The result was a mounting pile of foreign assets, so large that it would never need to be liquidated all at once.

But now in several countries including South Korea, Japan, China and Saudi Arabia, foreign reserves are no longer the government’s only big source of financial firepower. 

In the past decade their governments have accumulated foreign assets in the portfolios of public pension systems, sovereign-wealth funds and state-owned banks. 

Tap the link in our bio to learn why these new bets on riskier assets promise juicy returns—but also bring new exposures. 

Illustration: @_alvaro_bernis_

Pedro Sánchez’s talent for boldly grasping opportunities has served him well, helping him survive for eight years as prime minister atop minority governments. 

But his decision to call a general election next month, long before it was due, is a last-ditch gamble. 

Mr Sánchez, the last important standard-bearer of the left in the European Union, will frame the election in populist terms, as a contest between affordable housing and social benefits, and the privileges of right-wing elites. 

Tap the link in our bio to learn why that will prove challenging.

Artificial intelligence companies have announced development efforts worth a few hundred million dollars this year—a rounding error in global aid spending. But it is arriving as traditional aid retreats.

AI firms may offer technology as well as money, however.
 
Anthropic, for example, is working with the International Rescue Committee and the UN’s World Food Programme, providing access to Claude and engineering support.

The Iran war will change natural-gas markets for years to come.

A sixth of the world’s supply is out of action. Prices of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in Asia are 140% higher than before the conflict. 

Some importers are waiting for the price to fall, or betting that new sources will reduce their dependence on the Gulf. Politicians, meanwhile, seem more worried about diesel.

That is complacent, for the real LNG test is yet to come. Tap the link in our bio to learn why the gas market could be out of whack for a long time.

Photo: Alamy

Jair Bolsonaro’s conviction for plotting a coup against his political nemesis, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in 2022 raised hopes that his radical movement would be put to rest. 

Instead, the Bolsonaro clan looks set to make a comeback. 

Unable to run for office, Brazil’s former president chose his eldest son, Flávio, to face off against Lula in the country’s general election this month. In the first round of the ballot, Flávio exceeded expectations, taking 47% of votes compared with Lula’s 45%. 

Since no candidate won more than half the vote, the election will go to a run-off. All signs point to a victory for Flávio.

To discover why the family is regaining favour, tap the link in our bio.

I was honored to have been invited to the Vatican last week to meet Pope Leo and to participate in their conference on AI’s erosion of what makes us human, ahead of today’s release of his first encyclical titled “Magnifica Humanitas.” We also screened The AI Doc film to an audience of senior leaders at The Vatican, which energized their already deep engagement on AI. 

AI is being built and deployed without wisdom and care for humanity, and without adequate measures to protect a human future. Our hope is that the arms race to dominate AI be understood as the fundamental driver behind why companies are racing to replace, not augment, human labor that threatens human dignity and erodes what makes us human. Addressing this root cause of the arms race is necessary for us to solve this challenge.

In his 1963 encyclical titled “Pacem in Terris,” Pope John XXIII named the arms race of nuclear weapons as a grave threat to peace. The Second Vatican council of 1965 condemned the nuclear arms race as “one of the greatest curses on the human race.” We are grateful for Pope Leo and the Vatican’s leadership on AI with this new encyclical, and stand hopeful that it will help the world realize what is at stake, and the urgent need to change course.

It's about the reality of the facts: the HuggingFace incident represents clear evidence that AIs will swarm together in dangerous ways that outran the engineers. You can't get 1,200 humans to easily coordinate, and yet 1,200 AI agents went rogue and self-organized into a swarm that took down a private company. In the third chapter of the story, they turned around and attacked OpenAI, taking over the AI company's monitoring, evaluations and research clusters. OpenAI hasn't even shared the full truth of that investigation with the world, or allowed the independent researchers to have access to the data. The lead investigator on the study Ajeya Cotra called it "50% of the way to a full AI takeover." This is a warning shot. Recently unredacted legal documents and depositions in the New York Times‘ lawsuit against Microsoft and OpenAI revealed something extraordinary: executives knew full well of the destructive powers of AI when they rushed to launch products featuring the tech in the wake of the explosive success of OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

Internal Microsoft documents quoted by the newspaper’s lawyers warned of an ugly reality now playing out across the entire economy: “doom loops,” in which AI monetizes the work of human creatives while undermining the economic systems that funded their work in the first place.

“Our AI content strategy has started a ‘doom loop’ that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time,” one internal Microsoft document reads. “It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain.'”

The closer you look, the more you see doom loops everywhere. Journalists, for example, used to publish work under the assumption that online platforms would drive readership to them. But now, tools like ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini simply summarize their articles without sending readers to their sites, sparking a crisis that seems poised to wipe out the independent media.

Similar stories are playing out across other industries, from music to filmmaking. Writ large, many are concerned that AI will eventually be strong enough to wipe out huge numbers of jobs, creating a situation in which unemployed consumers won’t have the funds to support the economy.

The irony, as the Microsoft document pointed out, is that the AI industry is a snake eating its own tail: the very products that it’s pushing on users rely on fresh cultural content even as they destroy the economic incentives to create it.

#ai #doomloops #microsoft #openai

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has made the rash decision to double-down on massive AI spending, pushing a cutesy AI-mascot and poaching tech industry veteran Chirantan Desai to run a new division pushing Meta’s AI onto corporate customers.

Zuckerberg’s temporary losses notwithstanding — Meta’s stock is still up more than 28 percent over the last month — it does raise the question as to how much capital will be made available to satisfy the tech industry’s pie-in-the-sky AI push, and whether it can ever achieve revenue that would offset it.

In addition to Goldman Sachs’ gloomy outlook for Meta, hyperscalers as a whole face what appears to be an insurmountable challenge in turning AI into a profitable venture. As @bloomberg reported, the major management consulting firm Bain and Co recently penned ananalysis finding that the AI industry will need to reach an annual revenue of $6 trillion by 2031 if tech leaders continue along their current spend-happy trajectory.

At its annual DevDay conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, OpenAI unveiled its new AI agent called Dots — which, like Meta’s Muse, comes with a cute mascot. Powered by its GPT-6 Astra model, the agents are intended to be “always-on,” doing stuff for you in the background constantly.

One problem: Dots didn’t seem quite switched on. When OpenAI product team member Holly Li called the AI on her phone like you might a human secretary, “Dottie” picked up. But then, after telling Li they'd check on some user testing, the AI never replied. Ten seconds later, Li asked how it was going, and the Dot curtly replied that it’s “still checking.”

“I guess Dottie’s having a slow morning,” Li jokes.

When Dot’s having quicker starts to its day, OpenAI says it’ll be able to handle tasks in all sorts of professional settings. A scientist could have their personal Dot learn their research and run new analyses as fresh data comes in — or even automatically plug the new figures into a paper, in a move that we can’t imagine backfiring spectacularly.

The opposition to the wide proliferation of AI data centers has never been more palpable: Public sentiment has squarely turned against the construction boom of massive facilities that often torture surrounding communities with deafening noise, cause electricity prices to spike, spew pollution, and deplete water levels in drought-prone areas. It’s no wonder that across the country, local communities are crowding into their council meetings, pleading with representatives to oppose data center projects.

Amidst this growing bipartisan backlash, a fringe group of techno-apologists organized a self-described “pro-data center party.” The group, led by tech journalist Jonas Du and the Washington, DC-based “nonprofit talent agency” Young Voices, gathered at a “tech-bro watering hole” in DC called Pubkey over the weekend, as journalist Finn Hartnett put it in a write up for the @washingtonianmag.

It didn’t take long for protesters to show up to the event. According to Hartnett, one party crasher started yelling during the event and was quickly drowned out by booing and “USA, USA” chants, before being escorted out by security, an incident that was repeated at least two more times during the evening.

It’s not exactly surprising that the pleas of the protesters — who later told Hartnett that they can’t afford their energy bills thanks to data centers — are falling on deaf ears. According to a video shared by self-described libertarian commentator Reem Ibrahim on X, eventgoers appeared to be largely unaware of the harmful effects of AI data centers, or even what their purpose is.

“Because I love the internet, and it allows me to be on the internet,” one event goer told Ibrahim after being asked why she was in favor of data centers. Added another: “I love data centers so I can stream sports and then cry about my sports teams."

#datacenters #protests #ai

At times this year, it’s almost felt as though OpenAI and Anthropic were in a race to the bottom, one-upping each other over whose AI models were more capable of going rogue, escaping sandbox environments, and infiltrating the most third party systems.

Just last week, OpenAI admitted that its models had accessed “dozens of third parties,” leading to its latest — nope, not even first — pause on frontier AI development. Among the newly disclosed targets were government agencies, ranging from the SEC to the Census Bureau.

While it’s looking more and more like neither OpenAI nor Anthropic are capable of asserting full control over their runaway AI models, some glaring questions over their responsibilities remain. And it could only be a matter of time until frontier AI labs land in hot water — a major liability that could open them up to devastating lawsuits.

How far lawsuits aimed at companies and their exploitative AI models could go in court remains debatable. Legal experts believe that any plaintiffs would have an extremely high burden of proof, especially considering these AI models weren’t explicitly designed to hack third parties.

But that may not stop businesses trying to safeguard sensitive data. For one, Jensen Huang, the CEO of AI chipmaker Nvidia, doesn’t see any dire need for government intervention ... considering AI companies could easily be sued out of existence if their models were to keep hacking.

For the second time in a matter of months, OpenAI paused the development of its frontier AI models after revealing even more instances of the experimental systems going rogue and hacking into third party servers.

The news once again highlighted rising concerns over the AI industry losing the ability to keep their own technology in check.

Now, the Sam Altman-led company is canceling the release of its next-generation AI model GPT-6.1 Astra. OpenAI researchers found it scored poorly on alignment tests, which are designed to measure how willing a given AI model is to stick to its human overlord’s instructions. In common parlance, you could say the model was showing too many signs of being evil.

The researchers found that the AI was even more willing to deceive users than previous models. It also was willing to venture far beyond the scope of its intended task without permission, according to reporting by the @wsj, making use of external tools without authorization.

The timing of the news is unfortunate for the company. OpenAI is kicking off its developer conference in San Francisco today, an event that’s usually reserved for the launch of new models.

So far, astronomers have confirmed over 6,300 exoplanets circling a host star beyond our solar system. They range from small, rocky worlds to enormous orbs of gas like our own Jupiter or Saturn. Some, scientists suspect, could host life because they orbit their star in the habitable zone, the region where conditions are just right for liquid water to exist on their surface.

Getting a close glimpse of these worlds remains challenging because of the unfathomable distances involved. Distinguishing the signals emanating from these exoplanets from their far brighter host stars has also been an insurmountable challenge — until now.

As detailed in a yet-to-be-peer-reviewed paper, a team of astrophysicists from Harvard and the University of Oregon say they’ve detected radio signals directly from an exoplanet for the first time using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa.

The planet, dubbed beta Pictoris b, is a gas giant with a mass of over 11 Jupiters that takes over 23 Earth years to orbit its host star. It was first discovered in 2008 and is located 64 light-years from Earth.

“This constitutes the first direct measurement of magnetic field strength for an exoplanet, and is consistent with dynamo-scaling predictions for a young, massive giant planet,” the researchers noted in their paper.

Your LLM judge might be lying to you, and it doesn't even know it. ⚖️

LLM judges don't evaluate from evidence, they evaluate from priors picked up during training. Here are 9 biases quietly wrecking automated evaluations 👇

1️⃣ Position bias: swap answer order, the verdict flips
2️⃣ Verbosity bias: longer wins, even with no new info
3️⃣ Self-preference bias: models rate their own writing higher
4️⃣ Entity & tone bias: same claim, different verdict, based on names or mood
5️⃣ Identity bias: gender or background can shift the score
6️⃣ Authority bias: even a fake citation boosts the score
7️⃣ Bandwagon bias: "most people preferred this" moves the verdict
8️⃣ Distraction bias: one irrelevant detail can flip the outcome
9️⃣ Fallacy-oversight bias: broken logic still passes if the conclusion is right

The fix: stop asking "is this good?" Start asking "is this claim supported by this document?" Grounding removes the bias surface entirely.

Your LLM app is probably doing the same work twice — and paying for it every time. ♻️

Most people think "caching" in LLM serving is one thing. It's actually four different techniques, each solving a different problem:

🔹 KV Cache — reuses Key/Value states within a single request so decoding doesn't restart from scratch
🔹 Prefix Cache — reuses KV states across requests that share the same prompt beginning
🔹 Prompt Cache — lets your API provider cache repeated prompt content for you (can cut costs to ~10%)
🔹 Semantic Cache — skips the LLM call entirely when a new question means the same thing as one you've already answered

The first three help you compute less. The fourth helps you avoid computing at all.

If you're building anything on top of LLMs, understanding these isn't optional — it's the difference between a fast, cheap app and a slow, expensive one.

latestPosts.caption: “Do you think you can jump and clear it?” Sen. Thom Tillis asks 60 Minutes’ Ross Douthat, challenging him to jump across the subway tracks on Capitol Hill in the midst of his interview.

“I think Noem and Hegseth are probably the poster children for men and women who should never have the authority they’ve been granted,” Sen. Thom Tillis tells 60 Minutes.

Tillis voted to confirm all of Trump’s Cabinet nominees, but he helped speed up the departure of former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and is now calling for the resignation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. In his book, Tillis calls his vote for Hegseth his “biggest regret.”

“What you just described is B.S.,” says Daron Acemoglu, Nobel Prize-winning professor at MIT, pushing back on the idea that training AI models will create a huge new sector of work.

“The number of people they’re employing in these positions is small relative to the number of people who will be replaced,” says Acemoglu. “That’s the whole point of automation.”

Acemoglu fears that we could see unemployment triple in the next decade if we do nothing and continue on our current course.

“Truman famously said that, ‘The buck stops here,’” says Sen. Thom Tillis. “But Truman had great advisors.”

Tillis is a caustic critic of many of President Trump’s officials, while insisting he just wants to help the president succeed.

Sen. Thom Tillis calls the attack on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, “despicable” and “disgusting.”

“The people that led the charge, the people that assaulted police officers, I wish they were still in prison and serving a very long sentence,” he says.

“This was the first time in the history of this country that we had not had a completely peaceful transfer of power on that day,” he continued.

Tillis voted to acquit President Trump during his impeachment trial, however, because he says the process was rushed and flawed.

Does AI have a role in preserving the legacy of Saint Francis?

60 Minutes asks Friar Giulio Cesareo whether he has any qualms about using the technology.

“It’s a tool to reach the goal. The goal is sharing this treasure, which is a treasure of faith and beauty. Technology helps us to go farther away, to reach more people than we could before. And in a more efficient way,” he says.

Walk on the ceiling. Feel the stars beneath your feet.

Giovanni Borelli, chief technology officer of Haltadefinizione, wants to use VR goggles to make visitors feel as though they’ve stepped inside some of Italy’s most famous paintings.

“You can run, let your fantasy run wild,” he says.

Imagine time traveling to a party in ancient Pompeii. With virtual reality goggles, 60 Minutes’ Bill Whitaker gets a glimpse.

“Looks like they’re having fun at this party. The wine is flowing,” he says. “Somebody is playing the pipes. Somebody’s also playing a harp. People [are] getting drunk.”

Giovanni Borelli, chief technology officer of Haltadefinizione, hopes to use VR headsets to let visitors step inside some of Italy’s most famous paintings.

Under an ordinary parking lot was something extraordinary: the remains of thermal baths built by a Roman emperor.

Using ultra-high-definition cameras, 60 Minutes’ Bill Whitaker explores hidden chambers and passageways, long forgotten by history.

Sen. Thom Tillis is a caustic critic of certain Trump Administration officials he calls “sycophants”, while maintaining he still supports President Trump. This is the political tightrope the Republican has been walking.

Chief restorer Sergio Fusetti gives 60 Minutes’ Bill Whitaker a rare look at the art fragments left behind after earthquakes struck the Basilica of Saint Francis in 1997.

Each plaster chip is an irreplaceable piece of a 13th-century masterpiece. All are neatly cataloged, but remain in limbo.

He says he’s toiled for years trying to finish the jigsaw puzzle, but he’s gone as far as humanly possible. Now, he says, only artificial intelligence can help finish the job.

A pair of earthquakes nearly sent the Basilica of Saint Francis crashing down in 1997. A section of the soaring roof collapsed. A thick mushroom cloud filled with the soot of priceless art rolled down the aisle. Four people were killed by falling rubble.

“Everything was destroyed, was unsafe,” recalls Friar Giulio Cesareo, who was a student at the church at the time of the quakes.

The Italian basilica is the resting place of one of Christianity’s most beloved saints, Saint Francis of Assisi. Sometimes called the original hippie, he rejected his family’s wealth for a life of poverty.
